questions.stem: A telecom's billing-dispute agent hands a case to a human specialist whenever a disputed amount exceeds its authority. The escalation rate is about right. Specialists say each escalated case still takes around 12 minutes, because they have to reread the whole chat and re-query the billing system before they can act, and customers end up repeating themselves. Which change would MOST improve the escalation step with minimal changes to the agent?

options.text: Lower the escalation threshold so that specialists receive disputes earlier, before the conversation with the customer has grown long and hard to follow.
Have the agent write a structured handoff at escalation: account, disputed charges and amounts, what it checked and found, why it escalated, and a suggested action.
Attach the complete raw transcript and every tool result to the ticket automatically, so that specialists always have all of the available information in one place.
Tell the agent to keep working with the customer for several more turns before escalating, so that fewer disputes reach the specialist team in the first place.

questions.explanation: The escalation rate is fine; the cost is in the handoff. The person picking up an escalation usually has not seen the conversation, so the agent should hand over a concise, structured summary of who the customer is, what is disputed, what has already been checked, why it is escalating and what it recommends. That lets the specialist act immediately and spares the customer from repeating themselves. It changes only what the agent outputs at the escalation point.

whyWrong.A: Escalating earlier changes which cases reach specialists, not how quickly they can act on them. The rate was already appropriate, and specialists would still have to reconstruct each case themselves.
whyWrong.C: More raw material is not the same as usable context. A full transcript plus tool dumps is exactly what specialists are already wading through; they need the case distilled, not appended.
whyWrong.D: Delaying escalation for cases beyond the agent's authority frustrates customers and does nothing to shorten the specialist's work once the case arrives.

questions.mindset: An escalation is only as good as the context it hands over; design the handoff for someone who never saw the conversation.

questions.stem: A retailer's support policy states that customers can always reach a human. The Claude support agent is set up to escalate only after it has tried to resolve the issue itself. Logs show that when customers write "I want to speak to a person," the agent asks three or four more diagnostic questions first, and satisfaction scores for those chats are very poor. What should the architect do?

options.text: Make an explicit request for a human an immediate escalation trigger in the routing rules, and pass the agent's case summary along so the customer does not repeat anything.
Add few-shot examples in which the agent politely explains that it can usually resolve the issue faster than a human, then continues with its diagnostic questions.
Score the customer's sentiment on each turn and escalate only when the frustration score passes a threshold, so that calm requests are still handled by the agent.
Let the agent finish its diagnostic questions before escalating, so that the human specialist receives a complete case and can resolve it on the first contact.

questions.explanation: Policy says the customer can always reach a person, so an explicit request is itself the escalation trigger; it should not be second-guessed or delayed. Honour it straight away, and keep the value of the work done so far by handing over a summary.

whyWrong.B: This tries to talk the customer out of a right the policy grants them. It is a prompt tweak that makes the policy violation more polite, not compliant.
whyWrong.C: Sentiment is a poor proxy for whether escalation is required. A calm customer who asks for a person is just as entitled to one as an angry customer.
whyWrong.D: This is the current behaviour that is producing poor satisfaction. The customer already said what they want; extra questions delay a guaranteed handoff.

questions.mindset: When policy grants the user a human on request, the request is the trigger. Do not make them earn it.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company has medical reviewers approve Claude-drafted responses to inquiries from healthcare professionals. The approval rate is 97% and reviewers spend about three minutes per item, so the dashboard looks healthy. The QA lead wants hard evidence that reviewers actually catch errors, not just that they spend time on each draft. Which approach gives the MOST reliable evidence?

options.text: Survey reviewers every quarter about how carefully they read each draft and how often they find problems, and report the results with the approval-rate trend.
Have a second Claude instance re-review every approved response and count each case where it disagrees with the human approval as a missed error by that reviewer.
Mix drafts containing known, planted errors into the normal queue without labelling them, and track each reviewer's catch rate alongside approval rate and review time.
Enforce a minimum review time of five minutes per draft before the approve button is enabled, so that every reviewer is guaranteed to read the draft in full.

questions.explanation: Approval rate and time-per-item measure activity, not effectiveness. Seeding the queue with drafts that contain known errors gives you ground truth: you know what should have been caught, so you can measure a real catch rate per reviewer and spot automation bias or fatigue early.

whyWrong.A: Self-reported diligence is not evidence. Reviewers who are rubber-stamping usually do not realise it, and a survey cannot reveal what they missed.
whyWrong.B: A second model's disagreement is not ground truth. It may be wrong itself, so its disagreements mix real misses with its own errors and cannot measure reviewer performance reliably.
whyWrong.D: A timer forces time spent, not attention paid. Reviewers can wait out the clock, and it adds cost without producing any evidence that errors are caught.

questions.mindset: Measure human review with ground truth: plant known errors and track the catch rate, not just approvals and minutes.

questions.stem: An insurer's underwriters review Claude-drafted risk summaries and fix them in a free-text editor before approving. Six months in, the same kinds of errors, such as missed flood-zone exclusions and wrong policy limits, still appear at the same rate, and underwriters' editing time has not fallen at all. Which TWO changes would BEST turn the review step into a source of continuous improvement? Choose TWO.

options.text: Capture each correction in structured form, recording which field changed, the type of error and the corrected value, rather than keeping only the free-text edit.
Ask underwriters to rate each summary from 1 to 5 for overall quality, so the team can track a single satisfaction trend line for the summaries over time.
Move to a larger, more capable model, because error categories that persist for six months show that the current model lacks the capability for this task.
Add representative corrected cases to the evaluation set, weighted toward the most frequent error types, and re-run it whenever the prompt or model changes.
Append every mistake underwriters have ever reported to the system prompt as a growing list of things to avoid, and update that list once every week.

questions.explanation: Reviewer edits are the richest signal the system produces, but free-text edits are invisible to engineering. Structured correction records show which errors are frequent, and feeding corrected cases into the eval set lets the team test prompt or model changes against exactly those failures, closing the loop from human review back to the system.

whyWrong.B: A single quality score says the summaries are bad without saying what is wrong, so it cannot guide a fix.
whyWrong.C: Changing models without measuring the error categories is a guess. The errors might come from missing context or prompt design, and there would be no eval to show whether the new model helped.
whyWrong.E: An ever-growing list of past mistakes in the prompt is untested and unmeasured. It bloats the context and gives no evidence that any error rate actually went down.

questions.mindset: Human corrections are training data for your process; capture them in structured form and feed them into evals.

questions.stem: A data-platform team lets an agent clean up stale customer records across three databases. A human approves each run, but the approver sees only the agent's own description, such as "will archive inactive accounts older than two years," after which the agent runs its queries freely. Last month a run archived active enterprise accounts because the agent misread a date field. What should the architect change so the approval is meaningful?

options.text: Have the approver read the agent's full reasoning trace after each run is complete, so that mistakes like a misread date field are spotted and reversed more quickly.
Require the agent to state its confidence in how it interpreted each field, and abort the run automatically whenever that self-reported confidence drops below 0.8.
Add a second human approver for the agent's description of each run, so that two people must agree that the stated cleanup plan is sensible before execution.
Have the agent first produce a dry run listing the exact records and changes; the human approves that change set, and execution is limited in code to the approved set.

questions.explanation: The approver was approving intent, not the actual effect. A dry run turns the plan into a concrete, checkable change set, such as which accounts and how many, so a human can spot that enterprise accounts are in scope. Constraining execution to exactly that approved set means the agent cannot do something different from what was reviewed.

whyWrong.A: Reviewing after execution turns a gate into an audit. The damage to active accounts has already been done by the time anyone looks.
whyWrong.B: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the agent that misread the date field was presumably confident in its reading.
whyWrong.C: Two people approving the same vague description would both have missed the misread date field. Adding reviewers does not help when what they review hides the risk.

questions.mindset: Approve the concrete effect, not the stated intent, and make execution unable to exceed what was approved.

questions.stem: A mortgage-intake pipeline uses Claude to check applications for completeness and extract key fields. Anything not auto-cleared goes to a queue of loan processors. About 40% of that queue is applications missing a required document, such as a pay stub or proof of ID, and all a processor can do is email the applicant and wait. The queue is overwhelming the team. What is the BEST change?

options.text: Hire and train additional loan processors so that the team can absorb the current queue volume while still reviewing every application that is not auto-cleared.
Send missing-document cases straight back to the applicant with an automated, specific request, and keep the processor queue for cases that need human judgment.
Let Claude estimate the missing values from the applicant's other documents, so that more incomplete applications can be cleared without reaching processors.
Lower the confidence threshold for auto-clearing applications, so that more borderline cases pass automatically and fewer of them land in the processor queue.

questions.explanation: Human review is valuable where human judgment adds something. A missing pay stub is a data gap that only the applicant can fill, so routing it to a processor just adds a step. Sending a specific automated request back to the applicant clears 40% of the queue and keeps reviewers focused on cases that need a decision.

whyWrong.A: Adding headcount scales a badly routed workflow instead of fixing it. Processors would still be doing work that adds no judgment.
whyWrong.C: Inventing values that should come from required documents defeats the purpose of the completeness check and puts unverified data into a lending decision.
whyWrong.D: Lowering the threshold lets more uncertain cases through automatically, which raises risk and does not help, because incomplete applications still need the missing document.

questions.mindset: Route each case to whoever can actually resolve it; humans cannot fix missing data either.

questions.stem: A legal-tech startup is building a consumer app in which Claude drafts answers to tenants' questions about eviction notices and lease disputes. To keep costs low, the founders want answers delivered straight to tenants with a prominent "this is not legal advice" disclaimer. Considering Anthropic's Usage Policy, what is the BEST design?

options.text: Treat this as a high-risk use case: have a qualified legal professional review the content before it reaches the tenant, and tell users that AI is involved.
Keep direct delivery, make the disclaimer more prominent, and require tenants to tick a box confirming they understand that the answer is not legal advice.
Have a trained customer-support agent read each answer for tone and obvious mistakes before it is sent, and state in the app that AI helps produce the answers.
Add a second Claude instance prompted to act as a senior housing lawyer, and send each answer to the tenant only after that reviewing instance has approved it.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's Usage Policy treats consumer-facing advice in domains such as legal matters as high-risk. In those cases a qualified professional in the field must review the content before it is disseminated, and users must be told that AI is being used. Tenants facing eviction are exactly the people the requirement protects. The professional review step is a workflow gate, not an option.

whyWrong.B: A disclaimer does not satisfy the requirement for professional review, and a vulnerable user is likely to act on the answer regardless of the label.
whyWrong.C: The disclosure part is right, but the policy calls for review by a qualified professional in that field. A support agent is a human in the loop without the qualification the requirement is built around.
whyWrong.D: A model reviewing a model is not a qualified professional. It adds cost while leaving the human-review requirement unmet.

questions.mindset: For high-risk consumer advice, a qualified human reviews before release; disclaimers and model self-review are not substitutes.

questions.stem: An ops team runs a headless agent built on the Claude Agent SDK to triage production alerts overnight. It should read dashboards and logs freely, but calls to its `restart_service` and `failover_region` tools need the on-call engineer's approval via chat. Leadership wants the agent itself to carry out approved remediations to cut recovery time. The prototype bypasses all permission prompts and relies on a system prompt saying "ask on Slack before restarting anything." What is the MOST reliable design?

options.text: Keep permission prompts bypassed, but add a PostToolUse hook that posts to Slack after every restart or failover so the on-call engineer can roll back any bad change quickly.
Strengthen the system prompt with more emphatic wording and worked examples of asking before acting, and repeat the same rule in the project's CLAUDE.md for extra weight.
Use `default` mode instead of bypass, allow-list the read-only tools, and route the two risky tools to the SDK `canUseTool` callback, which asks on-call to allow or deny.
Remove the restart and failover tools from the agent entirely, so that it can only page the on-call engineer with a summary and a suggested remediation.

questions.explanation: The requirement is a hard gate on two specific tools, while the agent stays autonomous for everything else. In the Agent SDK, a tool call that nothing earlier in the permission flow has approved reaches your `canUseTool` callback, which pauses execution until your code returns allow or deny, so it can post to on-call and wait. Allow rules let the read-only tools run without ever reaching the callback. The bypass mode has to go (run in `default` mode, which has no mode-based auto-approvals), because auto-approved calls never reach `canUseTool`; the gate lives in the permission path the model cannot talk its way past.

whyWrong.A: A PostToolUse hook runs after the tool has already executed. A notification after an unapproved regional failover is not an approval gate.
whyWrong.B: Prompt and CLAUDE.md instructions guide the model but do not enforce anything. With permissions bypassed, nothing stops the call if the model misjudges.
whyWrong.D: This would be safe, but it ignores the stated goal that the agent itself carries out approved remediations to reduce recovery time.

questions.mindset: Put the approval gate in the tool-permission path the agent cannot bypass, and only on the actions that need it.

questions.stem: A treasury agent prepares outgoing wire transfers, and any wire above a set amount needs approval from a treasury officer in a mobile app. Overnight, approval requests often go unanswered and time out after 30 minutes. To make sure vendors are paid on time, a product manager proposes that timed-out requests should execute automatically. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Accept automatic execution on timeout, but record every auto-executed wire in a dedicated log that a treasury officer reviews first thing each morning.
Execute timed-out wires automatically only when the agent reports high confidence that the payment is legitimate, and hold all of the remaining ones.
Hold timed-out wires, but let the agent clear its own request when the payee is on the approved-vendor list and the amount matches an open invoice.
Keep timeouts failing closed so no wire is sent, escalate unanswered requests to a backup approver rota, and track approval latency against a published SLA with alerting.

questions.explanation: An approval gate that opens on timeout is not a gate: the riskiest moment, when nobody is watching, becomes the moment the control disappears. Fail closed, and fix the real problem, which is approver availability, with a backup rota and latency monitoring.

whyWrong.A: A wire transfer is hard to reverse; reviewing it the next morning is an audit of money that has already left the account.
whyWrong.B: The agent's self-reported confidence is not a calibrated control, and a fraudulent or erroneous wire may look legitimate to the agent.
whyWrong.C: The actor whose action needs approval cannot approve it. A vendor-list match and an invoice match are exactly what a compromised vendor record or a duplicated invoice would also pass; the officer exists to catch those.

questions.mindset: A required approval must fail closed; solve availability with escalation paths, not by auto-approving.

questions.stem: A content-moderation team has human reviewers adjudicate posts that Claude flags as possible policy violations. Their decisions also become the labels used to build the evaluation set and calibrate the flagging threshold. An audit finds that two reviewers given the same post agree only about 60% of the time. Which TWO actions BEST address this? Choose TWO.

options.text: Let Claude make the final call whenever two reviewers disagree, because the model applies the written policy in the same way to every post it sees.
Write a decision rubric with concrete examples for each policy category and its boundary cases, and hold calibration sessions on the items reviewers disagreed on.
Raise each reviewer's daily throughput target, so that far more labels are collected and the noise in individual decisions averages out across the set.
Show Claude's verdict prominently next to each post, so that reviewers' decisions converge on a single shared reference point and measured agreement improves.
Double-review a regular sample of items, track inter-reviewer agreement by policy category and by reviewer, and route persistent disagreements to a senior adjudicator.

questions.explanation: Low agreement usually means the criteria are ambiguous, and noisy labels then corrupt both the evals and the thresholds built on them. A rubric with boundary examples plus calibration sessions makes the criteria shared, and ongoing double-review with agreement tracking shows where ambiguity remains and gives hard cases a defined owner.

whyWrong.A: Handing disagreements to the model removes human judgment from the very cases that most need it, and makes the labels circular when they are used to evaluate that model.
whyWrong.C: Pushing for volume lowers care per item, and systematic disagreement caused by unclear criteria does not average out.
whyWrong.D: Showing the model's verdict anchors reviewers. Agreement would rise because people defer to the model, not because the judgments got better.

questions.mindset: Human review needs shared criteria and measured consistency before its labels can be trusted as ground truth.

questions.stem: A hospital has signed a BAA with Anthropic and enabled HIPAA readiness for its Claude API organization. The product roadmap lists five changes for workloads that process PHI. Which TWO proposals are NOT eligible under HIPAA readiness and must be redesigned before they touch PHI? Choose TWO.

options.text: Moving the nightly discharge-summary job to the Message Batches API to roughly halve the cost of the large overnight batch run.
Calling the token counting endpoint on each prompt to estimate request size and cost before the message itself is sent.
Giving the patient-question agent the web fetch tool, so it can pull pages from drug-information sites while it composes answers.
Sending scanned referral letters to the Messages API as PDF documents, so that Claude can extract the referral details from them.
Using structured outputs with a fixed JSON schema that contains no patient data, to extract discharge fields in a consistent form.

questions.explanation: HIPAA readiness covers only the features marked eligible in Anthropic's feature eligibility table, and the API returns a `400` error for requests that use a non-eligible feature in a HIPAA-enabled organization. Batch processing (which retains results) and the web fetch tool are listed as not HIPAA-eligible, so those PHI workloads need a different design, such as synchronous Messages calls or keeping PHI out of the job. Token counting, PDF support and structured outputs with a PHI-free schema are eligible.

whyWrong.B: Token counting is listed as HIPAA-eligible, so estimating cost on PHI prompts is allowed under the arrangement.
whyWrong.D: PDF support is listed as HIPAA-eligible for PDFs sent inline through the Messages API, which is what this proposal does. Uploading them through the Files API would be a different matter.
whyWrong.E: Structured outputs are HIPAA-eligible. The rule is to keep PHI out of the schema itself, which this proposal already does.

questions.mindset: A BAA covers eligible features only; check every feature in a PHI path against the eligibility list before building.

questions.stem: A health insurer's Claude API organization has HIPAA readiness enabled under a signed BAA. Its engineers also use Claude Code with API keys from that same organization to work on the claims-adjudication service. To reproduce a tricky bug, a developer proposes pointing Claude Code at a copy of the production database containing real member records. What is the BEST response?

options.text: Allow it, because Claude Code used with API keys from a commercial organization is eligible for zero data retention, so Anthropic will not store any member records it sees.
Decline it: Claude Code is not covered by HIPAA readiness, so reproduce the bug with synthetic or properly de-identified data and keep PHI stores out of its reach.
Allow it on condition that the developer runs Claude Code in plan mode, so that it can read the member records but cannot modify anything in the database copy.
Allow it after adding a CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude Code never to print member names, dates of birth or ID numbers anywhere in its terminal output.

questions.explanation: Anthropic's documentation states that Claude Code is not covered under HIPAA readiness, which applies to eligible Claude API features. Real member records would therefore flow into a tool that the arrangement does not cover. The safe path is synthetic or properly de-identified test data, plus access controls that keep production PHI away from developer tooling.

whyWrong.A: ZDR is a separate arrangement this organization may not even have, and retention is not the question: HIPAA coverage comes from the BAA, and the docs explicitly exclude Claude Code from HIPAA readiness.
whyWrong.C: Read-only access still sends PHI to an uncovered tool. The compliance problem is the data flow, not the risk of modification.
whyWrong.D: An instruction about output does not stop PHI from being read and sent as context. It is a prompt-level mitigation for a data-flow problem.

questions.mindset: Compliance coverage is per product and feature; developer tooling is a data path too.

questions.stem: An EU online lender wants Claude to make small-loan decisions from end to end, approving or declining in seconds. Legal points out that GDPR restricts decisions based solely on automated processing that significantly affect people, and that Anthropic's Usage Policy treats financial decisions about individuals as high-risk. Product insists on keeping decisions fast. Which design BEST meets the obligations while protecting speed?

options.text: Have a credit officer empowered to change the outcome review each decision before it is final, working from a Claude-prepared case summary, and give applicants reasons and a way to contest.
Keep decisions fully automated, but add a sentence to the privacy notice explaining that an AI system is used in assessing loan applications and naming the model provider.
Keep decisions automated during the day, and have a credit officer click to approve the full batch of the day's decisions each evening so that a human has signed off on every one.
Remove name, nationality and other protected characteristics from the decision prompt entirely, so that the automated decisions are demonstrably fair and therefore fall outside the GDPR restriction.

questions.explanation: Two obligations point the same way. GDPR's restriction on solely automated decisions with significant effects can be relaxed only with safeguards such as the right to human intervention and to contest, and Anthropic's Usage Policy independently requires a qualified professional to review high-risk financial decisions before they are finalized. Claude can still deliver most of the speed by preparing a concise, evidence-linked summary, so the officer's review is quick but real. The officer must have the authority and information to change the outcome; otherwise the decision is still effectively automated.

whyWrong.B: Transparency is required, but telling people about a solely automated decision does not provide the human involvement the rules call for.
whyWrong.C: Bulk sign-off on a day's decisions is a rubber stamp. Nobody actually reviews the individual cases, so the decision remains effectively automated.
whyWrong.D: Removing protected attributes may reduce bias, but fairness does not change the fact that the decision is solely automated and significant.

questions.mindset: For significant decisions about people, use AI to speed up a real human decision, not to replace it with a token sign-off.

questions.stem: An external auditor is reviewing a bank's Claude-based customer email assistant. They ask the architect to demonstrate how each obligation is met: US-only data residency, retention limits on logs, access control to transcripts, and human approval of any outbound message about credit decisions. The team currently has a policy document describing the controls it intends to have. Which deliverable BEST satisfies the auditor?

options.text: The model provider's own compliance reports and certifications, showing that the provider of the model has been audited against recognised security frameworks.
The system prompt, which includes an instruction for each obligation, together with a set of sample transcripts showing the assistant following those instructions.
A narrative architecture document that explains the design intent behind each control in detail, formally reviewed and signed off by the CTO and the CISO.
A control matrix mapping each obligation to an implemented control, its owner, and evidence such as workspace geo settings, retention config and approval records.

questions.explanation: Auditors need proof that controls exist and operate, not statements of intent. Mapping each obligation to a named control, an accountable owner and a verifiable evidence artifact, such as exported residency settings, log-retention configuration, access reviews and approval records, is the standard governance deliverable and makes gaps visible.

whyWrong.A: The provider's attestations cover the provider. They say nothing about the bank's own logs, access controls or approval workflow.
whyWrong.B: Prompt instructions are not enforceable controls, and a few good transcripts are anecdotes rather than evidence that a control operates consistently.
whyWrong.C: A signed design narrative is still a description of intent. It provides no evidence that the controls are implemented and working.

questions.mindset: Compliance is demonstrated by obligation-to-control-to-evidence mapping, not by intentions, prompts or a vendor's badge.

questions.stem: A European insurer wants to build an evaluation set from 5,000 real customer claim emails and send them to an external labeling contractor, who will write the gold-standard answers. The emails contain names, home addresses, health details and policy numbers. Which TWO steps are MOST important before any data leaves the company? Choose TWO.

options.text: Have Claude produce the gold labels itself instead of the contractor, since a provider under contract is not a third party for this data.
Pseudonymise or redact the identifiers in the emails and strip health details the labeling task does not need, keeping any re-identification key inside the company.
Encrypt the files with a strong password before transfer, and send that password to the contractor in a separate email from the one with the data.
Confirm the lawful basis and sign a processing agreement covering purpose, retention, deletion and onward sharing, then log the dataset in the data inventory.
Select emails only from customers who have already closed their policies, because data about former customers is no longer covered by GDPR at all.

questions.explanation: Evaluation datasets are a personal-data flow like any other. Data minimisation means sending only what the task needs, with pseudonymised identifiers and special-category health data removed unless it is essential. Sharing with a contractor needs a lawful basis and a processing agreement that limits purpose, retention and onward transfer, and the dataset must be inventoried so that access and erasure requests can find it later.

whyWrong.A: Model-generated gold labels defeat the purpose of an independent evaluation set, and sending the data to any provider is still processing that needs a basis and safeguards.
whyWrong.C: Encryption in transit is good hygiene, but the contractor still receives full, unminimised personal and health data once the files are opened.
whyWrong.E: Former customers are still data subjects. Their personal data remains protected after the policy relationship ends.

questions.mindset: Eval sets and labeling vendors are part of the data flow: minimise first, then contract and inventory.

questions.stem: A European telecom collected chat transcripts to resolve support cases, and its privacy notice describes only that purpose. Marketing now asks the AI team to run Claude over three years of transcripts to build per-customer upsell profiles, including inferred household income and life events. Technically, this is a quick batch job. What should the architect do FIRST?

options.text: Have marketing add profiling to the privacy notice and publish the update, then run the job, since customers will have been informed before any profile is built.
Run the job, but instruct Claude never to infer sensitive attributes such as health, religion or political views when it builds each customer's profile.
Pause and take it to the DPO and legal: a new purpose and profiling need a compatibility check, a lawful basis and likely an impact assessment before processing.
Remove customer names from the transcripts first, then proceed, because profiles keyed only by customer ID number no longer count as personal data under GDPR.

questions.explanation: Data collected for support cannot simply be reused for marketing profiling. Purpose limitation requires assessing whether the new purpose is compatible and establishing a lawful basis, and profiling customers at scale is the kind of processing that typically triggers an impact assessment and updated notices. The technically easy path is not the first step; governance is.

whyWrong.A: Updating the notice is transparency, not authorisation. It does not make reuse of already-collected data compatible with the original purpose or supply a lawful basis, and the assessment has to come before the notice is rewritten, not after.
whyWrong.B: Limiting which attributes are inferred is a useful safeguard later, but it does not provide a lawful basis for the new purpose.
whyWrong.D: Data keyed by customer ID is pseudonymised, not anonymous. It still identifies people and remains personal data.

questions.mindset: A new purpose for existing personal data is a governance decision before it is an engineering task.

questions.stem: A US federal agency runs a Claude-based case assistant on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) under its FedRAMP High authorization. To improve retrieval and debugging, a developer adds a commercial SaaS vector database and a commercial LLM-observability service, neither of which is FedRAMP authorized. Both receive case text containing Controlled Unclassified Information. The model endpoint itself stays in GovCloud. What should the architect do?

options.text: Treat both services as sitting outside the authorization boundary, and replace them with options authorized at the required impact level before any CUI flows to either one.
Keep both services in place, since the FedRAMP authorization covers the model endpoint, which is where the sensitive processing of the case text takes place.
Keep both services, but require TLS in transit and encryption at rest for each of them, which together satisfy the FedRAMP High control baseline.
Replace only the vector database, since it stores case text at rest, and keep the observability service because it receives transient copies of prompts rather than a persistent store.

questions.explanation: A FedRAMP authorization belongs to specific services and environments. Running the model in an authorized environment does not extend coverage to other components. Every service that stores or processes the CUI must sit inside an appropriately authorized boundary, so the vector database and observability tool must be replaced with authorized alternatives or kept away from CUI, and the system documentation updated for the authorizing official.

whyWrong.B: Authorization does not flow outward from the model endpoint. The vector database stores the CUI and the observability tool receives it, so both are in the data path.
whyWrong.C: Encryption is one control among many in a baseline. It does not turn an unauthorized service into an authorized one.
whyWrong.D: Transient receipt is still processing of CUI outside the boundary, and most observability tools retain what they receive anyway. Both services are in the data path, so both must be authorized or kept away from CUI.

questions.mindset: Authorization covers environments, not data flows; every component that touches the regulated data must be inside the boundary.
